title: The speck and the plank (Matthew 7:1–5)
hookLine: judge not; take the beam out of your own eye first

cards: Someone in the group chat says something, and before you've finished reading it you've already written the review in your head. Tone-deaf. Typical.
Who does that? It's fast, it's easy, and honestly, it feels a little good.

Now Jesus, still on the hillside, turns from worry to this, with a picture so absurd it's meant to make you laugh: a man with a whole wooden beam sticking out of his eye, leaning in close to help his friend with a speck of sawdust.

teach.b: It opens with one of the most quoted lines in the Bible, in the King James: "Judge not, that ye be not judged."

Then the reason: "For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again." The ruler you use on other people is the ruler that gets used on you.

Then the picture: "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" A mote in Greek is a karphos, a tiny chip, a bit of straw or sawdust.

teach.h: A CHIP AND A ROOF BEAM.
teach.b: The beam is a dokos, a roof timber, the kind that holds up a house.
Mark calls Jesus a tekton, a carpenter or builder, and this sounds like a builder's joke: the biggest piece of lumber in the shop, jammed in your own eye, while you squint at your friend's splinter.
Judge not doesn't mean never tell right from wrong.

Verse six asks for discernment, and verse five ends like this: "Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye." Then. After.
The speck is real, and helping with it is allowed.
But the order matters: first, your own eye. The Greek word hypocrite meant a stage actor, someone playing a part; here, the part of the judge. And there's a quiet mercy in it.
When you've just wrestled with your own beam, you tend to be gentler with someone else's speck. You know how it feels to have something in your eye.

how: Many Christians examine their own conscience before correcting anyone else, and some churches build a quiet moment of self-examination into worship before confession or communion.

o: a judge's ruler for measuring others' faults
a tiny chip of straw or sawdust in the eye
a roof beam, the big timber that holds up a house

games.q: what's in the picture — tap the pairs.
p: a chip, a bit of sawdust

s: judge not means never tell right from wrong
verse five ends with helping your brother: "then shalt thou see clearly."
the beam is a big roof timber
the Greek dokos is a beam that holds up a house.
hypocrite first meant a stage actor

games.q: your friend has a speck of sawdust in his eye. you'd like to help. what does Jesus say to do first?
o: take the beam out of your own eye.
games.why: "first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly." helping is allowed. the order matters.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has irritated you lately, and name the speck: what they did. Then gently ask one question, not to beat yourself up, just to look: is there anything like that in me?
Maybe a plank, maybe a splinter, maybe nothing; sit with whatever you find, and if you pray, you can ask for clear sight.

wordCard.voice: Dokos, the Greek word for a roof beam, the biggest piece of lumber in the shop. A chip of sawdust in their eye, a roof beam in mine, and the beam comes out first.

orig.note: Greek: a beam, a roof timber; the King James beam, today's plank.

carryVoice: Your line: the plank first. Then you can see clearly enough to help. Until tomorrow.
